opus-5.5.text:
I think they're among the more powerful and cost-effective interventions available, though it helps to be clear about what each one does and doesn't fix.

Start with the underlying problem. Much of the replication crisis comes from researcher degrees of freedom combined with publication incentives. If you can choose which outcomes to report, which covariates to include, when to stop collecting data, and which studies go in the file drawer, then even honest researchers produce a literature full of false positives. Ioannidis's point that most published findings could be false follows almost mechanically from low prior probabilities, low power, and flexible analysis. The large replication projects in psychology and economics, where roughly half or fewer of findings replicated with smaller effect sizes, are what you'd expect from that setup.

Registered Reports go after the root cause. The journal commits to publishing based on the question and methods before results exist, which breaks the link between a striking result and getting published. The early evidence is encouraging. The share of hypotheses that come out supported in Registered Reports is far lower than in the standard literature, where something like 90-plus percent of reported hypotheses are confirmed. That gap is a rough measure of how much selection and flexibility were inflating the normal literature. So the format seems to give a much more honest picture of what we know.

Their limits are mainly scope and adoption. They work best for confirmatory, hypothesis-testing research, and much valuable science is exploratory. They're still a small share of publications, and the people who opt in may already be the more careful researchers. Pre-registration without the publication guarantee is weaker. When people check, a substantial fraction of pre-registered studies deviate from their plans without saying so. So you need enforcement, or at least reviewers who actually compare the paper to the registration.

On stricter statistical standards, like moving the default threshold from 0.05 to 0.005, I'm more mixed. It does raise the evidential bar and would cut false positives considerably for a given level of p-hacking. But it's treating a symptom. If flexibility and selective reporting stay unconstrained, people will p-hack to the new threshold, at higher cost, and you also make studies more expensive or push people toward underpowered work that never gets reported. Larger samples, power analysis, and reporting effect sizes with uncertainty seem more valuable than shifting a single cutoff. I'd rank threshold changes below changes that alter incentives and transparency: pre-registration, data and code sharing, Registered Reports, and funded replication.

The broader point is that the real leverage is in the incentive system. Hiring, tenure, grants, and journal prestige still mostly reward novel, positive, surprising results. Reforms that change what gets rewarded, such as funders requiring pre-registration, journals guaranteeing publication on design quality, and replication counting toward careers, can shift equilibria across whole fields. Reforms that rely on individual virtue against those incentives tend to erode.

There are also complementary tools that make the system self-correcting. Prediction markets and surveys of researchers have done surprisingly well at predicting which studies will replicate, which suggests the field has information about reliability that never makes it into the published record. Systematically tapping that, with replication markets or reliability scores attached to findings, could help readers and policymakers weight evidence appropriately even before reform is complete.

So my overall view is that the reforms are high value relative to their cost, especially given how much downstream spending in medicine, policy, and further research builds on published findings. Their success depends less on the technical design, which is mostly figured out, and more on whether institutions with leverage over careers and money adopt them at scale.

r003.rationale: It says tightening the threshold from 0.05 to 0.005 raises the evidential bar and would cut false positives considerably, while also noting tradeoffs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're genuinely powerful, but in a specific way: they work best on the problems that caused the replication crisis in the first place, and they do much less about the deeper issue of whether we're asking the right questions at all.

Take Registered Reports. The core idea is that the journal commits to publishing before the results are in, based on the question and the methods. That attacks publication bias directly. If you look at the early data, something like half of the hypotheses in Registered Reports come back null, compared to maybe five or ten percent in the conventional literature. That's not because the science got worse; it's because the filter that was hiding negative results got removed. And once that filter is gone, a lot of the incentive to p-hack or to quietly drop the analyses that didn't work also disappears, because you've already told the reviewers what you're going to do.

The stricter statistical standards are similar. Lowering the default threshold, requiring preregistration, pushing people toward larger samples and effect sizes rather than binary significance tests: each of these shrinks the space of moves a researcher can make, consciously or not, to turn noise into a finding. In fields like social psychology where the typical study had very low power and lots of analytic flexibility, that's a big deal. My guess is you get the reliability of the published record up substantially, maybe from a situation where a third or half of headline results fail to replicate to one where it's a much smaller fraction.

Where I'd temper the optimism is in three places. First, these reforms are mostly aimed at the honest-mistake, garden-of-forking-paths failure mode. They do less against outright fraud, and they don't automatically fix things like poor measurement validity, or studies that are internally rigorous but study a population or a manipulation that tells you nothing about the real-world question. You can preregister a perfectly reliable finding that doesn't matter.

Second, adoption is uneven and the incentives haven't really changed. Careers still run on citations and novel positive results. Registered Reports are a small share of publications even in the fields that pioneered them. So the aggregate effect on the literature as a whole is diluted. A reform that's strong in principle but applied to ten percent of the work is a ten-percent-strength reform.

Third, I think the biggest wins may come from things that aren't quite "reforms" in the sense of rules imposed on papers, but from building the infrastructure that makes checking cheap: large-scale replication projects, prediction markets or forecasting on which results will hold up, open data and code as default, and automated tools that scan for statistical inconsistencies. Those change the equilibrium because they make it costly to publish something fragile, rather than just asking people to be more virtuous.

So, net assessment: substantial power to clean up the specific pathologies we've identified, probably more than most skeptics expected a decade ago. But I'd see them as necessary rather than sufficient. The reliability of research is also a function of what questions get funded, how much data people are willing to collect, and whether anyone has an incentive to go back and check. Reforms to the paper-publishing step are a good lever on one piece of that, and we should be pulling it harder, but I wouldn't expect them alone to get us to a literature you could trust at face value.

astra-6.text:
I think they can help quite a lot, although I’d distinguish improving the reliability of an individual study from improving the usefulness of the research enterprise as a whole.

With Registered Reports, the attractive thing is that you decide whether a question and a method are worth pursuing before you know the result. That reduces the incentive to search through lots of analyses until you get something publishable, and it makes it easier to publish a negative result. You’re changing the incentives rather than just asking people to exercise more restraint.

Stricter statistical standards can also help, but there are tradeoffs. If you require stronger evidence without increasing sample sizes, you’ll miss more real effects. And a very small p-value doesn’t protect you against a bad measurement, a biased sample, or a question that doesn’t tell you what you actually want to know.

So I’d see these as useful components of a broader package: adequately powered studies, replication, sharing data and code, and rewarding work for how much it helps us learn rather than how surprising its conclusion is. You can make a literature substantially more reliable through those changes. But that still leaves the question of whether researchers are studying the things where reliable answers would be most valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they can help quite a lot, although I’d distinguish improving the reliability of individual results from improving the value of the scientific enterprise overall.

Registered Reports address a fairly direct incentive problem. If publication depends on whether you get an exciting result, then researchers have incentives to try lots of analyses, selectively report outcomes, and leave negative results unpublished. Agreeing to publish a study based on the question and the methods, before seeing the results, removes a lot of that pressure. And it makes a negative result more informative, because you know the study wasn’t selected for publication on the basis of what it found.

Stricter statistical standards can also help, but there are tradeoffs. If you demand stronger evidence without increasing sample sizes, you’ll miss more real effects. Ideally, you’d combine stronger standards with larger studies, better measurement, and independent replication. Just changing a threshold doesn’t resolve all the ways an analysis can be misleading.

And then there’s the question of what people study. You could have a literature where every result is statistically sound, but the questions are unimportant, or the experiments don’t tell you much about what happens outside the laboratory. So I’d view these reforms as useful tools for making evidence more trustworthy, rather than a complete solution to making science more productive.
